paragraphs.text: FROM ORIGEN'S EXPOSITIONS ON THE PROVERBS OF SOLOMON.
CHAPTER 1.
A proverb is a hidden saying that is signified through another saying that is plain.

"For this reason he reigned in Israel: to know wisdom and instruction." Wisdom is spiritual knowledge. It contains the principles concerning God, incorporeal beings, judgment and providence, or it reveals the contemplation of ethics, physics and theology. Or again: wisdom is knowledge of bodies and of incorporeal beings, and of the judgment and providence that are contemplated in them. Instruction is the moderation of the passions, as it is observed in the passible or irrational part of the soul. And whoever devotes himself intently to theology has come to know wisdom.

That is, the faculty of judgment should be upright and undistorted. Someone who has no understanding of justice could not settle disputes rightly. Not even Solomon would have judged rightly between the prostitutes if he had not kept to the exact principles of justice. We shall judge rightly and without distortion if we obey virtue and condemn vice. There are three faculties of judgment in us: sense perception, reason and intellect. Sense perception judges sensible things; reason judges words and concepts; and intellect is the contemplation of intelligible things.

Just as the intellect apprehends sensible things through the senses, so through the virtues it beholds intelligible things. That is why the wise Solomon teaches us that the intellect holds the place of perception.

Those who acquire vice despise wisdom by the very fact that they are wicked. They do not have the fear that is the beginning of perception, so they become insensible and despise wisdom. How? By not practising it or pursuing it, for everyone who does evil hates the light. Wisdom is dishonoured not because of its own nature but because of their ignorance. The godly, however, choose instruction, so that once their soul is cleansed they may receive wisdom, which does not enter a soul that devises evil. But those who do not have the fear of God, which is the beginning of perception, are insensible to wisdom and instruction and despise them both. Such are those who do not accept the Old Testament and slander the Creator as cruel.

Just as the head and the neck here signify the intellect, so the crown and the necklace here signify knowledge. For this is the custom of the Holy Spirit: he has called God and his angels, the intellect, virtue, knowledge, ignorance, vice, and even the devil himself and his angels by many names. He does not apply these names at random, as some think. They are marks of different activities: God acting upon us through the angels, we acting in him, and demons acting against us.
These are co-heirs of the adversaries, since they share the same wickedness with them. And what they hold in common does not belong to the one God. Observe an evil concord, and its ruin.

The net is eternal punishment, a manifold penalty that the just Judge brings upon impure souls to destroy the wings that have grown wrongly. The winged creatures are we human beings, who have the power to fly upward if we will.

By "the ways out" he here means the soul that has gone out from vice and ignorance. Such was the exodus of the children of Israel, which came about after the new birth that comes from God's judgment and teaching. He also calls the same soul "broad": "Open your mouth wide," it says, "and I will fill it"; and Paul says in his letter to the Corinthians, "Open wide your hearts too." Wisdom is hymned by the soul that goes out in this way, and she speaks freely in a land broadened by the virtues. By "the tops of her walls" he means the highest dispassion, since those who love the law set a wall around themselves. David too prays for this wall when he says, "Let the walls of Jerusalem be built," that is, the parts of such a soul that have fallen down—evidently because of the affair of Uriah.

How then does Solomon say earlier, "Whoever rejoices over one who perishes will not go unpunished"? Or perhaps wisdom rejoices in the way she rejoiced at the destruction of Matthew the tax collector, and at the destruction of the thief who believed in Christ? For in the one case wisdom destroyed the thief, and in the other the tax collector.
Siege is moral teaching. It overthrows the soul that has been badly built, as God lays siege to it.

Just as infants are between the righteous and the unrighteous, so all human beings are between angels and demons until the end of the age. They are not demons, nor are they yet called angels. He said "they wronged infants," meaning those of whom Christ said, "Do not cause one of these little ones to stumble."
The dispassionate person rests without fear of any evil thought, and before long he will dwell in the kingdom of God, as one who has heard and kept his commands, because he hoped in him.
CHAPTER 2.
The one who hides God's commandment in this way is the one who does it, or who does not do it for vainglory. That is also why the demons are said to snatch it away: they do not allow us to do it.

Then you will understand how the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and how it brings about the knowledge of God, when in faith and longing you are in need of him. But wisdom and understanding must be there first, if one is to be able to understand the fear of the Lord. Let us put these words to those who despise wisdom and understanding and want to take refuge in fearing God as though it were something easy.

For if Christ does not rescue us, we shall walk the evil way as though it were good. The saints say everything trustworthy; others do not; and the devil says nothing trustworthy, that is, nothing worthy of belief. Here he calls the devil "a man," as in the Gospels, where "an evil man sowed the weeds." And the greatest snare, it seems, is to fall in with evil counsel and with deceitful, treacherous and wicked men.

If this evil counsel, which is crushed, that is, darkened, is a movement of the intellect, how could it forsake the teaching of youth? And how could it forget the divine covenant? For he speaks to us of evil counsel as though it were a rational living being. Or perhaps he here calls the devil "evil counsel," since the devil took evil counsel when he said, "I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High." He forgot divine knowledge and abandoned the teaching of youth. This youth refers to his former state, in which he was even enviable. And if wisdom can bring understanding to the young, among whom there is much unruliness when it is absent [?], it is all the more useful to an old man.

Those who are overtaken by years of life through the works of the everlasting life to come are the ones who lay hold of the straight paths of the untroubled and unbroken life. They are not overtaken by his mercies into the paths of the straight everlasting life [?]. — For the Lord loves those who pursue righteousness, and the counsel of the evil one will not overtake them. But those who have trusted in the devil do not lay hold of the straight paths of life, nor will they return to the kingdom of God.
CHAPTER 3.

The one who forgets the law is the one who does not live lawfully. The one who remembers the law is the one who lives by it. The one who keeps God's words is the one who not only does them but also counsels others to do them. And the one who destroys them is the one who is unwilling to practise them and hinders others, for it is not the hearers of the law who will be justified.

Healing is the health that virtue brings to your way of life, and care is God's grace and attention to your thoughts and reflections. When the powers of the soul, that is, the virtues, receive care, then all my bones will say, "Lord, Lord, who is like you?" For when the soul's power of memory receives care, it will surely say, "I remembered God and was glad." Likewise the power of sight will say, "I considered your works and was amazed." So too the power of desire: "Lord, all my desire is before you." And the power of reason will say, "I considered the days of old." The same will be true of the other powers.

That is, for those who are willing it holds nothing difficult, as the desire for money does. A pure intellect draws near to wisdom, since it knows what is good; but the impure intellect will be kept far from it.

After the transgression Adam was prevented from partaking of this tree, since the tree of life is planted from the fruits of righteousness, and the tree of life is the wisdom of God. Every lawless person is justly prevented from touching this tree.

God founded the earth by wisdom, and by his perception the depths broke open and the clouds poured down dew. What he here calls earth, the holy Paul called breadth. What are here called heavens, Paul calls height in his letter to the Ephesians. The depths, so called figuratively, he calls depth, and the dew-laden clouds he calls length. All these are symbols of rational natures, which are distributed into worlds and bodies in proportion to their state. This also applies now to the Son of God. But the faithful soul too is earth that bears fruit a hundredfold. It is made wise by richness, which is wisdom, as God founds it upon her. For he establishes it, making the gathering together of its teaching and its firmness out of wisdom. And as it keeps advancing, he makes it heaven, a most pure creation, the dwelling of angels and of intelligent beings. It has received perception of what truly is and understands the exactness of things, that is, the manifold richness of God's judgments.

Against wisdom alone the demons are powerless, since they are not permitted to cast thoughts into the heart of one who has been made wise. For the intellect that lays hold of the contemplations of wisdom becomes closed to impure thoughts. — A pure intellect draws near to wisdom, since it knows what is good; but the impure intellect will be kept far from it.
The stumbling block of the rational nature is an impure thought or false knowledge. But whoever is fenced about by God's counsel does not stumble on these.

Neither the assault of evil thoughts, he says, will frighten the one who has become wise, nor will the ungodly who attack from outside overthrow his strength in their wish to strip him of the things that are good by nature. For no one will be able to capture one who cannot be taken. And yet what is more arrogant than the ungodly? But you will prevail even over this beast of every kind, he says, if you are gentle and mild, for the Lord is with you. From this we learn that almsgiving drives away the frightening fantasies that come to us at night, or even during contemplation. Not only that: it also delivers those who are so minded from the evil accusations at their departure and from the harmful punishments at the judgment. Gentleness, freedom from anger, long-suffering and everything that naturally calms an agitated temper do the same, since frightening apparitions usually arise from the agitation of the temper.

Do not refrain from doing good to the needy, not only with food but also with the knowledge of God, with wisdom and with the commandments. Whatever is dear to God and draws one close to him, do not refrain from doing good with it to the one who needs you.

This enmity toward one's neighbour causes harm not only to the body but also to the soul. Ignorance of the Lord is in the houses of the ungodly, but the knowledge of God is in the souls of the righteous. The dwellings of the righteous are blessed when Christ distributes rewards to each according to their works, but the ungodly receive a curse and not a blessing.

Vice at its extreme, exalted to the utmost, is called pride. The Lord opposes the unjust as righteousness, liars as truth, and the proud as humility. That is why he is a friend to the humble-minded. This is the meaning of "He gives grace to the humble but opposes the proud."
Those who have learned and taught the divine wisdom will inherit heavenly glory. But the ungodly have heaped up for themselves dishonour from Christ before angels and men.
CHAPTER 4.

By "instruction" he means moral virtue, and by "understanding" divine knowledge. A son of the virtues is one who has been shaped by them and who does what accords with virtue for no other reason than for virtue's sake.

"I give you a good gift"—the heavenly kingdom—"if you do not forsake my law." It should be noted here that he calls the intellect a good gift, in contrast to the one who receives gifts unjustly in his bosom and does not prosper. For by those unjust gifts he means the things of the evil one; the intellect that receives them does not prosper in its ways.

The crown of graces is God's commandments, which in return grant the crown of the kingdom to those who keep them. The crown of delight is the knowledge of God, which shields us and drives off every passionate thought and all false knowledge.

These many ways lead to one way, the one who said, "I am the way." By "many ways" he means the virtues that lead to the knowledge of God. The years of life will be multiplied for the one who hears the heavenly Father through the prophets and receives his words through the only-begotten Son, so that he is directed in the ways of righteousness in this life and may be saved into everlasting life.
The place of this army is vice, knowledge falsely so called, and anything at all that is unacceptable to God. For the enemies are the ungodly thoughts that kill souls.
The Lord gives sleep to his beloved. But the ungodly are not his beloved, so the Lord does not give sleep to the ungodly. From this one can also argue plausibly that demons by nature do not sleep.

The virtues go before us and illuminate us in this present life, which is called night in comparison with the life to come, which is day—until the day is established on which the Sun of righteousness rises. Or the meaning may be that they do not leave us until they set us in safety, for it is proper to day to dispel darkness. This is what Christ said: "Whoever walks in the day does not stumble." The ways of the ungodly are the opposite. Since they did not know or understand, they walk in darkness. They stumble, but they have no excuse, as if they stumbled through ignorance, for they made the darkness for themselves. See how virtue made light even in darkness, while vice made darkness even in light. — The ungodly do not know even how they sin, nor do they know the cause of their stumbling. They do not even know this very thing, that they are breaking the law—which is the mark of the utmost wickedness.

By springs he means the virtues, from which flows the living water of the divine words, which is the knowledge of Christ. And David says, "The springs of the waters were seen, and the foundations of the world were laid bare"—that is, at the coming of our Saviour Jesus Christ.

"Let your eyes look straight," he said. That is, let them look at what alone is dear to God: what the prophets have made clear to us about Christ alone and his disciples, and whatever anyone may say that draws one close to Christ, and nothing else.

With these words agrees the saying, "Unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city." That is, unless the Lord gives us the strength to direct our steps toward him, we labour in vain if we do not call on him in supplication but set about things in self-will.
CHAPTER 5.

For both open prostitutes and the teachings of heretics prattle on, deceiving the hearts of the innocent with fair speech. So the greatest safety is not to be caught in the first place, for once caught it is hard to escape.

Their sweetness goes no further than the ear. The fat signifies pleasure, from which impurity is born. Its offspring are vice and ignorance, and on the day of judgment nothing more bitter than these will be found among all created things.

From this we learn that the irascible part predominates in demons. "For their anger," it says, "is merciless, and their wrath sharp." They hunt down to destruction those who obey them; that is how they honour those who honour them.

Through their vices the wicked wear away the flesh of Christ and squander his blood, regarding it as common. For he says, "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day." But whoever eats the body and drinks the blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself.

There was a time when evil did not exist, and there will be a time when it will not exist, for the seeds of virtue cannot be wiped out. I am persuaded of this also by the rich man, who was "almost" but not completely "in every evil": he was judged in Hades for his wickedness, yet he took pity on his brothers. And showing mercy is the finest seed of virtue.

Knowledge is both a well and a spring. To those who are approaching through the virtues it seems a deep well; to the dispassionate and pure, a spring. So too the Saviour sat by the spring at about the sixth hour. Take the spring to mean the divine knowledge, and not a well of water. A spring gives forth without labour, that is, it offers running water to the thirsty, whereas a well yields water only with labour to those who wish to draw. And just as a spring never stops flowing, so the literal sense of Scripture keeps its course and makes it easy for the thirsty to honour God. And just as a well demands labour from those who draw from it, so does contemplative knowledge from those who wish through it to achieve the virtues of soul and body, to understand divine things, and to lay hold of the kingdom of heaven.

Here "wife" signifies the knowledge of God. She was given to us from our youth, and above Solomon calls her the teaching of youth. For he says, "Son, let not evil counsel overtake you" (meaning the devil, who took evil counsel), "which has forsaken the teaching of youth and forgotten the divine covenant." Forgetting and forsaking come after the acquiring of knowledge, just as disease comes after health and death after life. Note also that this same knowledge is called mother, wife and sister. She is mother, since the one who taught me begot me through her, as Paul begot the Galatians through the gospel. She is wife, because by living with me she bears virtues and right doctrines, since "wisdom bears understanding for a man." She is sister, because she and I have come from the one God and Father. For it says, "Say that wisdom is your sister."

Grace and friendship set free; virtue and knowledge set free the rational soul. For grace and friendship are virtue and knowledge. And if the deer is born of friendship, the colt is born of the graces. The deer, then, is the symbol of contemplation, and the colt of dispassion, for the one naturally arises from the virtues and the other from knowledge. — The deer is a symbol of the contemplation of bodies and incorporeal beings and of the knowledge of God. Friendship is a symbol of love toward God and neighbour, and the colt of dispassion. Contemplation that leads to the knowledge of God usually arises from the virtues of the soul; love naturally arises from wisdom; and dispassion from the virtues of the body. He urges us always to keep company with such graces, and whoever delights to dwell with them will not only keep company with God but will also come to share his home. — Proper to the rational nature is the virtue called friendship, which makes those who follow it friends of God through the knowledge of God. — For whoever walks in the company of the friendship of virtue and of knowledge will be benefited many times over.

Some think this is said about the wisdom of outsiders, with which it is not good to linger because of the deceptions it contains. Others take it to refer to vice and to not spending much time with it, interpreting it as follows: it is altogether impossible for a person to keep free of evil thoughts, but it is possible not to linger in them. These he calls "arms."
CHAPTER 6.

Everyone who gives surety for his friend Christ, who is righteousness and truth, hands his own soul over to the enemies who are accustomed to make war on human beings, because of his friendship with the Saviour. For spiritual friendship is knowledge of God, and it is by this that the saints too are called friends of God: John the Baptist was the friend of the bridegroom, and so were Moses and the apostles. "For no longer," he says, "do I call you servants, but friends."

Do you see the struggle and the wakefulness? Sleep is the soul's sin in act. Drowsiness is the first impure thought that forms in the soul. Slumber is the inclination toward worse things. The law, then, forbids sleep, and the Gospel forbids drowsiness, since the one cuts off sin in act and the other cuts off the wickedness that first forms in the mind. "For it was said," he says, "to those of old, You shall not murder; but I say to you, You shall not be angry."

It should be noted here that he calls the ant's natural and harmonious movement wisdom, for it is even said to be "wiser than the wise." But how can it not be under a master, if all things are servants of God? Or perhaps God is called master in two ways: as creator, and as the one who is known? This is why Paul writes: "But now that you have been set free from sin and enslaved to God" (that is, by virtue and knowledge), "you have your fruit unto sanctification, and its end is eternal life." If the ant, being irrational, has no share in such an end or in knowledge, then it is clearly also free of that kind of servitude. So the ant is rightly said not to be under a master in respect of this mastery. Yet it is also said to be under mastery, under God as its creator.

Through the ant Solomon seems to sketch for us the practical way. Through the bee he signifies the contemplation of created things and of their Maker himself, which pure and impure, wise and foolish alike take for the health of the soul. The wax seems to me to stand for the things themselves, and the honey stored in it to be a symbol of their contemplation. The wax will pass away, for "heaven and earth," he says, "will pass away," but the honey will not pass away, for neither will the words of our Saviour Jesus Christ pass away. Of these words Solomon says: "Honeycombs are good words, and their sweetness is healing for the soul." And David says: "How sweet your sayings are to my throat, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" He has given the name "labour" to the outcome of the labour of the virtues and of knowledge. By "kings and commoners" he does not mean those who wear the diadem or the poor on the dunghill. Rather, he calls "kings" those whose mind has been made wise toward God and strengthened by the virtues. This sleep can befall only a rational soul, for here it signifies ignorance and lack of knowledge. Wakefulness from these makes a person like a sparrow alone on a housetop.

It should be considered here whether it is perhaps through such movements of the body that the adversaries recognize their own thoughts turning about within us, since we believe that God alone knows the heart.

Everyone who eats the flesh of Christ and drinks his blood (1) acquires righteous blood. A rational soul deprived of it is said to die: "For the soul that sins, it shall die." And if there is righteous blood, there is clearly also unrighteous blood. Those who devour the food given to the peoples of the Ethiopians, and are fed on the bread of falsehood, gather this blood within themselves. Those who sacrifice to foreign gods use up their own righteous blood, but those who offer themselves as a sacrifice to the one God destroy the unrighteous blood. And upon the destruction of the unrighteous blood there will surely follow [?]. This is indeed how things now naturally happen, but from the beginning it was not so. For children do not gain health through the destruction of disease, since they are born with health from the beginning.

By slandering them to one another with falsehood, he drives them into disputes and lawsuits. Or else: the brothers are those who have the gift of adoption and are under the same father, Christ. The witness of injustice tries to separate them by casting disturbances and judgments among them. The word "kindles" is added, I think, because of passionate thoughts, which inflame anger toward wrath and hatred, and desire toward shameful deeds. Holy Paul also called these thoughts the flaming darts of the evil one, which wound the soul and bring about death.

He commands that the mother be led along. She is wisdom that gives birth, the wisdom that is according to God. Yet he ought to have said the father, since the father is better suited to be with the son. But since it is impossible to know God himself before contemplating created things, he commands that the mother, and not the father, be led along, so that through the mother the son may see the father. For unless she gives birth, he does not see the light, which is the knowledge of God himself. — The commandment of the law is a lamp and a light. Perhaps the lamp is the Old Testament, for that was "the lamp that burned and shone," and the light is the New Testament, for "I," he says, "am the light of the world." It is a reproof of evil and an instruction in good, for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.
For the pleasure of wickedness is worth as much as a single loaf.

If he is caught by true knowledge, he will put away all false knowledge. He is the one who formerly stole, through lack of knowledge, from the knowledge and wisdom that our Saviour made foolish. He is said to repay sevenfold, which means praising God seven times a day. And by giving God all the senses he has, he will rescue himself from the punishments prepared for the devil and his angels.

Everyone who has shared in wickedness is an adulterer against the devil, who first wedded wickedness and was a murderer from the beginning. Along with him, such a person brings destruction on his own soul.
CHAPTER 7

Wisdom is our sister because the Father who made the incorporeal nature also made her. Here he means by wisdom not the Son of God, but the contemplation of bodies and incorporeal beings, and of the judgment and providence contained in it.

Here he calls human flesh a window. Through it the evil one works his deceptions on people, on those who wish to walk the broad and spacious road that leads to destruction. Here we should pay attention to what Solomon says about wickedness. At first she does not lead a person to the broad street, nor does she compel him to go through the passages of her houses, or to approach a corner, or to talk in the darkness of evening. But if she sees someone giving himself over to pleasures, she at once meets him in the guise of a harlot, which makes the hearts of the young flutter away.

Those who roam in the streets take in thoughts of adultery, fornication and theft. Those who roam outside them pursue pleasures contrary to nature, seeking to lie with males and taking in fantasies of certain other forbidden things. But beware lest this become a charge against holy men too. Anyone who does not keep stillness but roams about will share in the charges laid against the dishonourable woman.

Some thoughts are pure and others impure. Likewise, some lines are called straight and others broken, and a corner is a straight line that has been broken. Understood spiritually, the corner is the impure thought. So when wickedness lies in wait at every corner, this shows that she deceives the soul through all the impure thoughts.

By the bed-cords, the saffron and the rest he signifies deceptive speculations, or the various passions. — See how wickedness has no beginning of her own, but begins from the preliminaries of virtue, for to take someone as a partner in a sacrifice is a good thing. But once she has overcome them in the wrestling, she injects her venom by listing the things lovers desire. All of these are able to bewitch, not by their own nature, but because of the folly of those who hear. In the spiritual sense, wickedness seeks to put our face to shame through the bed-cords and the bed, the double-sided coverings, the saffron and the cinnamon. These signify evils and the various passions of pleasure found among the inventors of evil things.

"After many days he will return to his house." Paul looked with deep spiritual insight into the divine plan and says that the last enemy to be destroyed is death. Solomon described death beforehand as the husband of wickedness, the one who took humankind in his hand like a bag of silver. And yet, when people sin, he cannot disregard the fear of God, because God cares for the human race and bears with it. For if he had not kept the fear of God in view, he would have swept them all away [?]. — There are three kinds of heron: the one called the kemphos, the white, and the starred. Of these the kemphos is incontinent in mating. It beds down and mounts with difficulty, cries out, sheds blood from its eyes while mounting, and lays its eggs badly and with pain. From the natural history of this creature, Scripture seems to speak of those who yield to wickedness as made into kemphoi and likened to these birds because of their licentiousness. There is also another kind of kemphos at sea, which flies here and there in flocks. Sailors catch it by baiting a line with many hooks. It not only fails to flee when it sees the ones already caught, but each one races ahead of the other to be caught. Those who consort with wickedness are like this. Each hurries to outdo the other in pleasures, and so they impale themselves on a ruinous death.
CHAPTER 8
Here he has called virtue a "heart": the virtue that arises in the heart, or the spiritual heart that is created by God.

Here he has taken wisdom as the genus of instruction and knowledge. Having first set down instruction and knowledge, he adds, "For wisdom is better than precious stones," since instruction and knowledge are contained in wisdom. This wisdom is given through the Spirit as the word of wisdom, and the same thing is also called the spirit of adoption.
It should be noted that by injustice, insolence and arrogance he means the unjust, insolent and arrogant man, naming him after his worst habit.

That is, good counsel and safety come from me, for where the one is, the other is too. Do you see how everywhere incorporeal things are placed ahead of bodily things and rule over them? Then, having said that reigning itself comes about through her, he added something much greater: to be able to use rule justly, which is better than reigning. Some, however, take the kings to be the saints and the great ones, and the tyrants to be those who are still warring against the flesh and lording it over the passions.

Here he presents love as greater than friendship, when the two are not applied to the same thing. Indeed, when the Saviour said to Peter, "Do you love me?", Peter, knowing who was speaking with him, claimed the lesser for himself: "I am your friend." But when he heard the third time, "Simon son of Jonah, are you my friend?", he was grieved because the third time the Lord had assigned him the lesser (2).

The wise man alone is rich and glorious, for in him are an abundant possession and the fruits of wisdom. By sowing these to the Spirit he reaps life. When she speaks of her own wealth, she seems to be saying something like this: "You need no expense or novelty to win my love. It is enough simply to love, and you will be loved in return." Moreover, what is marvellous, that righteousness should be found in wealth, is also with me, together with all other good things.

The wisdom of God, being a substance, was begotten before the ages and was eternal before creation. But when it entered into relation with the things that come into being, it became the beginning of God's ways, the ways of making and of providing. "Beginning," then, is correlative to the creatures of which it became the beginning, meaning the relation to the things that come into being. But wisdom is eternal and exists in its substance with God before the ages.

Impiety is sin against God. But a person also acts impiously against his own soul when he heaps up for it the punishment prepared for the impious. It also follows that those who hate wisdom love death, since wisdom is life.
CHAPTER 9

Here one may take wisdom in two senses. I mean, first, the wisdom given by the Holy Spirit in words and writing to the godly-minded, through which the knowledge of God was also made known to the world. And likewise, second, the subsistent Son and Word of God, who brought all things from non-being into being by his wisdom.

Here he calls "victims" all the prophets who were sealed by Christ's exhortation and slaughtered. They mixed in the bowl of knowledge the knowledge of him, sweet as wine, for those of sound mind. He says, "Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul." For he himself made them victims and still does, because he urges those who believe in him to die for him, as he himself dies for you.

If Paul the apostle is a servant of Christ, and Christ is wisdom, then Paul the apostle is a servant of wisdom. We will apply the same argument to the other apostles and prophets too, and show them to be servants of his wisdom.

One should not reprove the wicked when they sin, but remind them of the fear of God, which will turn them away from wickedness. Or by "the wicked" he means those who are turning from sin and wish to come to repentance. While they are still wicked and blind, bear with them. Do not reprove them for every single fault, so that they do not turn to hatred at the very start. But when they have become wise and firmly established, reprove them. Christ, too, did not reprove the disciples while they were still young, because old wineskins are not fit for new wine. Or he calls "wicked" the senseless and foolish, or those wholly estranged from divine teaching, who must not be reproved but admonished and taught. And if Ahab and Herod were reproved, it was because they had already shared in the divine law, even though they transgressed it, and so they too had to be reproved. Or he seems to be saying this to the people of that time, who were more childish. Otherwise, why did John and Paul reprove? — One should not reprove the wicked when they sin, because reproof to someone's face makes the sinner more shameless. We should do this with the wise and righteous, and only between the one being reproved and the one reproving, not in front of many.

Whoever is carried about by every wind of doctrine has suffered shipwreck in the faith. He has shepherded himself and others as if under the wind, and so has perished. For he has abandoned the ways of the commandments of the one who said, "I am the vine, you are the branches, and my Father is the vinedresser." — Whoever does not gather divine knowledge together with the virtues does not gather the immortal fruitfulness of the eternal kingdom, and fruitlessness is wickedness and ignorance. To lay hold gladly of the divine words, which are like life-giving loaves, and of the divine thoughts found in the mind's hidden contemplation. — The loaves of the soul are the virtues, which our Saviour also commanded us to practise: fasting, self-control, prayer and the like. They are to be practised "in secret," so that people do not see them.
CHAPTER 10
By "a man" he means one who has become poor in the word, and by "hands" the deeds of wisdom.
The sensible man is not burned up by afflictions and misfortunes, and he bears the fruits of righteousness. But the lawless man is ruined even by better things.

By "unreproved instruction" he means the soul's evil way of life, which brings about its destruction and straying. The way of life, however, guards the guileless not only from eternal evil but also from every evil of life's hardships. By "the guileless" he means those who suffer evil at someone's hands and practise guilelessness in love. Or else: "unreproved" instruction is the kind that has the outward show of piety but is untrained and unexamined. For whoever is not reproved, and does not lay his thoughts and reasonings open to others, goes astray through conceit.

"Cover" means "do not let it raise its head." Or he calls wickedness "enmity," because through it we become enemies of God. The evil one produces in our hearts enmity against God and against people. The righteous shake it off, and whenever the evil one suggests such things to them, they hymn God with their lips. "For if while we were enemies," says Paul, "we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son." And if enmity is wickedness, then friendship is virtue and knowledge of God, through which we become friends of God and of the holy powers. In this friendship, those who are his friends are also friends of one another.

"Lord, all my desire is before you," says David. That is, we ought to desire what pleases God and befits the righteous, so that our prayer may be acceptable before God. But the ungodly man is carried off into eternal destruction by desiring and doing what is not dear to God.

If the fear of the Lord adds days, and the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, then these days are portions of wisdom brought about by the sun of righteousness. For as a person makes progress, he adds knowledge and illuminations. David prays for such days when he says, "Do not take me away in the midst of my days." Abraham too completed these days and died an old man, full of days. And the Lord adds divine visions, like days, to those who fear him in faith. But the years of the ungodly, shown to be without wisdom and without divine grace, were cut short.

He calls a person's lifetime an "age," as Paul does: "I will never eat meat, to the end of the age, so as not to make my brother stumble." For he gave the name "age" to the span that runs alongside the duration of his life. "For the righteous," he says, "will not give way to sin when he is harassed by the evil one." But the ungodly who sin will not only fall away from the kingdom, they will dwell in the fire and not on the earth.

That is, it is full of grace. By "the mouth of the godly" he now means the mind and the heart, which hymn God through the lips. But the mouth of the ungodly that speaks evil is turned away from God and belongs to the evil one. See what comes from the one and what comes from the other.
CHAPTER 11

Because the righteous man has his aim set on what is to come, when he dies he certainly obtains what he hoped for. Or else this points us to the resurrection. In the righteous man's case, what he has remains and does not vanish, but in the other's case even what he has is extinguished. For they boast only in the present age, and of them it is said: "Their glory is in their shame."

When he says, "The ungodly is handed over in his place," he does not mean that the godly man was liable to punishment. Rather, the snare is set by the evil one against the righteous man, and when the righteous man is rescued, the ungodly man falls into it. The godly man is snatched away by God, while the ungodly man is abandoned and falls in, as it is said: "The sinner was caught in the works of his own hands." Or else: since the righteous man, being human, is liable to some sins, when the ungodly man comes and does him harm, he frees the righteous man from his sins and from the punishments to come, and takes the penalties upon himself. And he is handed over by himself, by his own wickedness, since he has handed himself over to a debased mind.

That is, discernment about what should or should not be done, or the ability to manage one's own life. For life is a great and unbearable surge of waves. Such people are carried about by every wind and suffer shipwreck in their life or their faith. Those who lack the wisdom of God fall away from God like the leaves of a tree. And if salvation lies in counsel, and not merely in counsel but in much counsel, then no one is saved by bodies or by riches, or by nature, as those who posit natures claim.

Here he has plainly called the soul a body. Christ too names the soul "body" in the Gospels, when he says, "The lamp of the body is the eye." By the lamp he meant the mind, since it is what receives knowledge. By the body he meant the irascible and desiring part of the soul, which some call irrational and others passible. The one who does good, through the good he has done and teaches, gains for himself and his disciples knowledge of bodies and incorporeal beings in this life, and the kingdom of heaven in the life to come. But the other destroys not only his own body but also his soul, and he perishes in the fire together with those who follow him.

The one who lays hand upon hands unjustly is the one who becomes a teacher of evil deeds and doctrines. The one who sows righteousness is the one who puts forth words about the virtues and the knowledge of God.

Those who scatter what is their own and make it more are set against those who gather and are diminished. Those who scatter what is their own are those who sow to the Spirit and reap life. Those who gather and are diminished are those who sow to the flesh and gather corruption for themselves.

The grain is the divine word, which the Jews hid away and so left to the nations. — This is like what our Saviour says in the Gospels: "No one lights a lamp and puts it under the bushel; he puts it on the lampstand, to give light to everyone in the house." For as grain is food for the body, so divine knowledge is food for the soul. Whoever has the food of both and does not share it, but demands payment for them from those who have nothing to give, may he leave it to the demons. He also writes "cursed by the people," because on the day of judgment he will be cursed by the people of the angels and of all the righteous.

In the spiritual sense, carpentry is the practical working of the good virtues. The one who does what is owed to God seeks God-pleasing men who will receive what is owed to God [?], so that they too may trade with it as he does. But those who seek not good things but evil he will pass by.
This is the tree of life planted in the middle of paradise. After his sin Adam was forbidden to touch it, because he had cast away the seeds of righteousness from which the tree of life grows.
CHAPTER 12

"Do not be silent toward me," says David, "or I shall become like those who go down into the pit." A lawless man will be passed over in silence by God, that is, he will be hated and will not receive mercy, when God gives out the rewards to those who have received the grace of his incarnate dispensation. As he says in the Gospels: "And grace upon grace."
Chapter 13.

The wealth of the ungodly is wickedness. But the righteous will consume them, clearly through good teaching. So too in the age to come they will be set over fifteen cities. For the heavenly inheritance that those who gave themselves over to ungodliness were to receive, the righteous will inherit, as Paul also says: "By your hardness and your impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God." But the good one will give an inheritance to those who obey him as sons obey a father, and will adopt those who are his as sons into the kingdom of heaven.
Chapter 14.

[?] They are invincible, just as weapons provide safety. For nothing evil will stand against wisdom, because it is a weapon that cannot be fought down; against it alone the demons are powerless. But to the fool all things, both visible and incorporeal, are hostile.

Here he calls bodies "houses," for they are the houses of souls. The lawless ought to learn from those who know godliness and contemplative knowledge not only the knowledge of God but also the whole of the life-giving commandments, so that, having become pure, they may see God with the eyes of the mind. For this is the blessed end, which is kept for every rational nature. And the houses of the righteous are ready to receive everyone, as the Lord commands.

By "thoughts" he now means divine visions and the settled habits of the virtues, which he has set against the ways of a bold-hearted mind. For "out of the abundance of the heart the lips speak," said the Lord. The good man intends not to do evil but to do good. But the bold-hearted man, acting and speaking as a fool, will be filled with lashes and with the loss of his goods, and in the end he will lose his soul.
Chapter 15.

By "reproofs" he now means the commandments, for these reprove us when we sin. Those who hate them and die together with the shamefulness of their sins will waste away wretchedly together with the wicked inventor of sin. And by those who pass by wickedness [?] is made known [?]. Stillness is abstention from wickedness, both in deed and in visions, and in this the good keep still. But the eyes of the mind and body of the wicked devise evil all the time.

The prudent man is not in the Hades of sinners. The ways of life are the thoughts of divine words and works, and the prudent man always does and teaches these, so that, turning away from Hades together with those eager to learn, he may be saved.

Those who do not do his commandments are his enemies. But they become his friends when they run to the righteous, confessing their wicked deeds. Led on by them, they will walk the life-giving ways as the righteous do. As Paul proclaimed: "Those who were once enemies were reconciled to God through the death of his Son." Note that all enemies become friends through the righteous, so that Christ may say to all: "I no longer call you servants, but friends."
Chapter 16.

Again, here too there is need of wisdom, so that it may appease him. Or else the angel who knows the words concerning punishment is called the wrath of God. But the man who is wise in divine works and words, being of one mind with him, will not be terrified by him.

The nests of wisdom are the churches, or the tents in heaven; and wisdom is Jesus Christ, the Son of God. The nests of prudence, more to be chosen than silver, are the practical virtues: justice, knowledge, wisdom, temperance, courage, patience, forbearance, freedom from anger, almsgiving, and faith with hope and love. Through these, as by the rungs of a ladder, those who wish to go up and dwell there may enter the tents of wisdom without hindrance.

By "instruction" he means the fear of God, fasting, self-control, keeping vigil, singing hymns, and the discipline that comes upon us in sickness as God's testing. By "reproofs" he means the commandments of God, for these reprove us when we sin. Here he calls the senses "ways." Whoever guards them keeps his own soul from death for life. For Life is the holy Trinity, which gives life to all things and brought them from non-being into being. And whoever loves life and always longs to live in it will keep his mouth from words and works that are not of God, and will devote himself to the knowledge of God.

God is life. The fountain of the thrice-radiant Life itself is wisdom, knowledge, and the virtues. Those who drink from this fountain share in immortality and everlasting life. Those who possess such a fountain have understanding of the words of life. But the instruction of fools is wickedness, and instruction that does not accept reproof is folly.

He has called knowledge "discernment" because it recognizes all things. The heart of the wise understands what comes from its own mouth, both in judging bodies and incorporeal things, and in what they themselves teach others to do and do themselves.

The demons learn their words from the devil, attack the saints, and scheme to try to separate them from knowledge, which by its nature joins them in friendship with the heavenly powers. Solomon, I think, has shown this very thing through this proverb. By the "crooked man" he means Satan; by those "going about as lamps of deceit" he means the evil demons taught by him; and by "friends" he means the saints, who through knowledge are joined to God and to one another.

The lawless man is the devil. He tempts the friends of God and leads them away on roads that are not good but lead to destruction. When he deceives one of the saints, he fixes thoughts in his own eyes and devises perverse things, so that the one he has caught may not repent and be saved. With his lips he tickles that man's ears with every evil notion, with despair and every pleasure of licentiousness. He is a furnace of all wickedness, and in it he burns the souls of those who are going to fall. But the divine Spirit shakes off the flame of this furnace, whistling through it a wisdom like dew. And many wicked people still [?] are accustomed to imitate their father the devil.

Here he has called the hearts of the unjust "bosoms." And I think that everywhere the bosom signifies either the mind or knowledge. The devil takes the wicked into his bosom, but the Lord takes the righteous.
Chapter 17.

If everyone who commits sin is a slave, then everyone who has turned away from wickedness through virtue has mastered the demons, who are foolish masters. Such a person will also become a house of the mysteries of God, giving spiritual knowledge to each of the brothers in proportion to his condition. So too Paul gave milk to drink to those in Corinth, but fed those in Ephesus with more solid food, speaking of height and length and breadth and depth. By these dimensions he signified the division of rational nature, which contains the principles of God's judgment and providence; these are very deep indeed and lie beyond the human condition.
The furnaces are temptations. For through temptations God makes the hearts of the elect pure and spotless, and so chooses them.

The heretic listens to the tongue of godless doctrines, but those of the Church do not even pay attention. By "listens" he shows that this is voluntary, as of one who has sinned against the wise governance of God. — The one who listens to the tongues of the lawless is he who receives unjust thoughts from them and hastens to act on them. The righteous man is said not to pay attention to these, whether they come from the visible or the invisible, that is, not to nourish them in himself any further.

The faithful man, he says, will see the principles of this world, which he has figuratively called the "wealth" of the mind. But the unfaithful man will not know the principle of even the most ordinary thing, because of the impurity of his soul. That the wealth of the soul is the knowledge of God, Paul teaches when he says: "In everything you were enriched, in all knowledge and all wisdom." If anyone wishes to show that this is not the meaning of this proverb, let him say where those who went about in sheepskins and goatskins, ill-treated, afflicted, and distressed, had plenty of money. And how will the unbeliever not have even an obol, when many unbelievers are clothed in great wealth—I mean the kings and rulers of this world?

By "faithful lips" he means good thoughts. But to the fool evil thoughts will be welcome. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Unless perhaps he repents and receives prudence and faith.

Through justice we cover injustice, and through temperance licentiousness; again, through love we cover hatred, and through freedom from the love of money greed. We cover pride too through humility, and rashness through meekness, seeking spiritual friendship, which signifies holy knowledge. In Paul, too, some are said to have become fellow citizens of the saints and members of the household of the heavenly Jerusalem, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets.

Here he calls the body the house of the soul, and the soul in turn the house of the mind; and the same mind is in turn called the eye of the soul. Whoever has learned divine knowledge and wisdom but has given himself over to wickedness, bringing forth evil words instead of good, and not wishing to turn back and be saved—from his bodily house evil and wickedness will not depart. Rather, they stay firmly in it, so that the final evils may come upon him, remaining immovable in him on the day of the Lord's wrath. — Here he calls "house" the body fashioned for us by the Lord from the earth. And "will not be moved" means "wrath and affliction will not depart from his house," sent by the Lord through both men and demons against the one who has repaid evil for good to the man who did him good. — If he who repays evil for evil is lawless, how much more lawless is he who repays evil for good? Such was Israel in the wilderness, to whom Moses says in Deuteronomy: "A crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord?"

Here he calls knowledge the "beginning," and righteousness follows knowledge, for righteousness is born of knowledge. Want is ignorance, and strife and battle are all wickedness; and wickedness goes before ignorance. Why does he again find fault with the poor? To lead us away from idleness. So authority does not come from appointment; if you wish to walk with confidence, then, be righteous. "Strife and battle go before want": that is, for those who do wrong there is a want of virtue.
Like this is the one who calls bitter sweet and sweet bitter, and names light darkness and darkness light.

Here he calls wisdom and knowledge "wealth." But why should the fool have the learning of wisdom and knowledge? For just as a vine cannot grow in the sea, so wisdom cannot bear the fruit of virtue in fools. The wealth of the fool is the follies concerning each of his affairs; because of these he has become heartless and cannot acquire wisdom. — In every matter, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, for the Lord opposes the proud. And whoever is crooked about learning the things of God will fall into evils at the judgment.

Here he calls Christ a friend, who out of friendship for humankind became man. "For I no longer call you servants," he said to the disciples, "but friends." At every time, let Christ be with you as a friend. And if the sons of Christ are friends to one another, the angels and righteous men are brothers to one another, begotten by the Spirit of adoption. It is for this reason that they are begotten by wisdom: so that they may guide people from wickedness to virtue, and from ignorance to the knowledge of God.
The fickle man is the one who easily changes from virtue to wickedness, carried away by evil thoughts.

Here he calls God the father, and his love for humankind the mother, which also made him become flesh and endure sufferings for our sake. Our God and Father does not rejoice over a son who has been adopted but has not been instructed in the wisdom and knowledge of God, and has instead given himself over to wickedness and evil. But a prudent son gladdens his mother, God's love for humankind, which brings us to God the Father himself as sons who have been weaned and long for solid spiritual food, so that, just as his Son Jesus Christ became our brother by likeness, so we too may live our lives in deed and word. The Church is also our mother, whom God the Father has joined to himself as wife by the Holy Spirit; for through her he is always bearing sons and daughters for himself. Over those instructed in the knowledge and wisdom of God, both God our Father and the Church our mother rejoice. But over the uninstructed she is greatly troubled and grieves, since we do not wish to turn back and be saved, but remain in wickedness.

Here he calls contemplation the "face." For the contemplation of the thoughts of a prudent man is wisdom, knowledge, and righteousness. But the mental eyes of the fool are, even in drink [?], at the height of wickedness and evil.

Wrath is sent by God the Father against the foolish son on the day of judgment. And to the Church, which bore him by the Spirit, and to the choir of the saints, there will surely be grief at that time over the destruction of the foolish son. Note too that the prudent son has both one who bore him and a mother, while the fool has only one who bore him. For a mother is also one who bore, but one who bore will not always be a mother. If what was born dies in wickedness and ignorance, she is one who bore, but she is not a mother, because what was born did not share in the Spirit of adoption. The same will be understood of mothers in the sensible world and of bodily death: we shall call a mother also "the one who bore," but no longer the mother of a child who has died.

A man does wrong when he takes from the righteous what is rightfully his, or sins when he turns the righteous man's disciples toward injustice; for since the righteous man has them as his possession, he has suffered loss. "For they do not seek what is ours, but us." And by "rulers" he means those who reign in Christ.
Chapter 18.

The one who is led by the folly of the demons has no need of the wisdom or knowledge of God, because he loved darkness rather than light. And since he rejoices in folly, he thinks he has no need of wisdom.

As water gives life to plants, so the word of a man whose mouth has been sharpened by the virtues refreshes those who wish to be made wise and gives them wings toward God. By the "river leaping up" he means the indescribable wisdom of the graces of the all-holy Spirit, the ever-flowing wisdom of the thrice-radiant, single Godhead.

Whoever accepts the wickedness that belongs to the devil and acts according to it in contemplation and word shows partiality to the person of the ungodly. But it is neither good nor holy to pervert justice in judgment, in the account of bodies.
Rashness separates the soul from the meek and hands it over to death.

It is not the fear of God but the fear of the demons that casts down those who are sluggish toward repentance, for the demons rouse them to despair. Or else it is the fear of the Lord, which separates them from sluggishness and rouses them out of wickedness to repentance through good works. Effeminate in soul and body is the man who is dissolute and soft, who can neither teach himself nor wishes to learn from others. Or else: the fear of evils casts down beforehand those who are sluggish toward virtue, since they have nothing to give them courage regarding the future. A man who is womanish in his choices will not have the virtue that nourishes; and such people will go hungry when they see the kingdom from the opposite side, tormented in torment.

By "strength" he means the wealth of the knowledge of the Lord and the active power of the Word. For he alone knows the things that were before, the things present, and the things to come. He it was who gave the command, saying, "Let there be light"; heaven and earth and all that is in them were brought from non-being into being, and they show him to be the only Lord and God. Through an upright life the righteous run to him, and through contemplation they are exalted. Or else: from created things and their greatness, it is evident that God is almighty.

This saying should be used against those who have not received knowledge from God and yet try to teach others. For David says: "To hear the voice of your praise, and then to recount your wonders to others." And Solomon says: "What your eyes have seen, tell." For many who have not even made a beginning in virtue not only urge others to live rightly, but even force and command them to.

Here he calls God "a man." For whoever has served him by keeping his commandments calms his wrath toward himself at the judgment. The same holds for things of the sensible world. And just as our Lord is said to become a perplexed [?] leopard toward those who transgress, and a rock of stumbling toward those who do not believe, so too he becomes "faint-hearted" toward sinners. "Faint-hearted" can also refer to the evil one and to every demon that has fallen away from virtue and knowledge.

So he has called the upright life "a man's gift," which enlarges him and makes him worthy of the fullness of God. This he names the "seat of rulers," that is, of the holy powers. For the seat of the mind is the best settled disposition, which keeps the one seated on it hard to move or immovable.

Knowledge puts an end to folly, for it is the lot of rational nature. And it decides that something should happen among rulers, and they do it [?]; for everyone bows before the one who has divine knowledge. Or else: by "disputes" he here means the thoughts raised against us by the demons, which are opponents of virtue and eager to separate us from God. The lot of knowledge puts an end to these for us, and orders the ruling demons to withdraw, since the one who has it has been allotted to God, having divine knowledge both from God and from others [?].
Or else he means the soul, which is capable of receiving both life and death. From this is shown its free will to enjoy its fruits, whether good or evil, both now and in the future.
Whoever has found good wisdom has found the graces of God. — Whoever holds on to wickedness is foolish and ungodly, like the devil who invented it.
Chapter 19.

A wealth of knowledge and wisdom adds many angels to us. But the impure man, whom he calls poor, is separated even from the angel given to him from childhood. For spiritual friendship is virtue and the knowledge of God, through which we are joined in friendship with the holy powers, since people who repent become a cause of joy to the angels. So too the Saviour calls friends those who were once servants, having counted them worthy of his greater contemplation. So too Abraham, having grown rich in knowledge, sets that mystical table before his friends who appeared to him at midday. But Saul is separated even from the friend he had, because of his wickedness; for it is written: “And the spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord choked Saul.” By “the spirit of the Lord” he means the angel; for it says, “He who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flaming fire.” (9) That angels have been entrusted with human beings, the Lord teaches in the Gospels, saying: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels always behold the face of my Father who is in heaven.” And again Jacob: “The angel who delivers me from all evils.”

Those who do not know the principles of judgment and providence and blaspheme the Creator are false witnesses, and they will not remain unpunished on the day of judgment. And again, those who are troubled by their own passions and think that virtue cannot be attained bring an unjust charge against the one who gave the law.
Vulgar people do not show fear out of respect for rank; they are flatterers and show partiality. But the truthful man will not flatter evil; he will rebuke it.

Everyone who hates the poor brother, in the sense of “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” will be far from the love of God and of the angels. Or: everyone who hates a brother who is poor in virtue also keeps far from a life of friendship with the passions. — By “a good thought” he means the knowledge of God, and it is accustomed to draw near to those who know it, the pure in heart; and whoever obeys them so as to learn is prudent and will find it. — He who does much evil by deeds and words brings wickedness to completion, and wickedness is every sin; and he who brings to completion words against people for their destruction, and blasphemies against God, will not be saved.

Neither luxury of soul nor luxury of body benefits the fool. The first he will trample underfoot, being a pleasure-loving swine; and through luxury of the senses his flesh will be stirred to passions, and he will hurl blasphemies against God. Even if he goes from slave to free man, he will do this.

If whoever boasts rightly boasts in the Lord, and our Lord is wisdom, then whoever boasts rightly boasts in wisdom. The boast of the patient and merciful man, therefore, is his wisdom and knowledge; and it comes upon transgressors, freeing them from wickedness—now as something that may happen, but in the age to come of necessity.

Our Lord is a consuming fire and an angry lion. Toward sinners he burns and consumes, like wood, hay and stubble, the flesh that wars against the spirit; but toward those who do right he is light and dew, showing them the principles of created things, quenching the flaming arrows of the evil one, and cooling the burning heat that comes from practice.
He called the impure soul a harlot; and by her hire he meant her condition, from which prayers do not come out pure.

To teach sons about virtue and the knowledge of God belongs to fathers; but to give wisdom to children belongs to the Lord. For here he calls wisdom a wife; for he says: “Love wisdom, and she will keep you; honour her, that she may embrace you.”

The commandments are called commandments in relation to God who gave them; but in relation to the mind that travels in them they are called ways. He who keeps them guards his own soul, bringing it from death to life; but he who despises them will die the endless death.

So it is with things of the senses. But as far as the sun surpasses the moon, so far does the one surpass who has mercy on those in poverty of virtues and restores them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. By “giving a gift to God” he meant purity of heart; for in proportion to our dispassion we are counted worthy of knowledge by God.

What he says applies in this way to the affairs of this life. But I think that the great penalty means deprivation of the contemplation of created things, and the “adding of the soul” means the obliteration of the natural concepts of God, the soul having fallen utterly into irrationality. And the Saviour says in the Gospels: “What will a man profit if he gains the whole world, but loses and forfeits his soul?” Here “losing” indicates ignorance of bodies and incorporeal beings, while “forfeiting” represents the ultimate irrationality.

If the fear of the Lord leads a man to life, and the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction, then a man’s life is wisdom and instruction. To know wisdom and instruction, therefore, is to know Christ and his teaching. So the one without fear will dwell in wickedness and ignorance, where Christ is not. Those, then, who live in wickedness and ignorance do not look for the fear of God within themselves and do not hope for mercy upon themselves; nor is Christ in them, because they do not will it.

He who does not live rightly hides his hands in his soul unjustly, unwilling to work his own land—that is, the body—or to be filled with the breads of the soul. For the practical virtues serve as hands, bringing to our mouth the bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world through divinely inspired wisdom and knowledge.
CHAPTER 20

If their wine is the rage of dragons, and wine is a licentious thing, then rage is licentious, making people licentious; and anger is insolent, since it arises from seething rage. And if the Nazirites abstain from wine according to the law, then it has been laid down by law that the Nazirites are to be free of rage.
Here he has plainly called Christ king; for whoever provokes him by sins sins against his own soul.

Just as the fool is not ashamed of reproach, so also is he who borrows grain to sow at harvest-time, [?] already, since it will be repaid to the lender from his farm even if the borrower happens to die. — If it is possible at harvest-time to borrow grain from those who worked their own land in the six years—that is, to imitate the virtues of the righteous and the prophets who shone in the six ages before the coming of Christ, who also fed the widow and the orphans in the seventh year—so that the reward for displaying their virtues may be repaid to them in the kingdom of heaven, as those who became the firstfruits of the virtues.
Those, clearly, whom a man has begotten in virtue: the blameless man will leave them to those who come after as an image and a cause of blessing, along with a righteous upbringing to the end.

For elsewhere he said that the one who speaks evil dies. But also Christ: “And whoever speaks evil of the Church will be deprived of faith,” which was a light to him before his slander. He might also be speaking of the outer darkness, which is why it is said in the future tense. And Christ can be called both father and mother: father of those who have the spirit of adoption, and mother of those who need milk and not solid food. For indeed the Christ who spoke in Paul became father of the Ephesians, revealing to them the mysteries of wisdom, and mother (10) of the Corinthians, giving them milk to drink.
The pleasure devised for us by the evil one, which he calls “the portion at first,” fattens your throat for a time, but afterwards you will find it more bitter than gall.

Do not say, moved by pride, “I alone will fight my enemies,” but wait for the Lord and call on him to help you. Do not trust in yourself as though you could do anything without the Lord; for that there is no helper without him David says: “For I will not hope in my bow.”

Among things of the senses we speak of a large and a small weight, by which gold, silver, bronze, silk (11) and whatever else is weighed; and measures are for things measured in vessels: grain, wine, oil and pulses. But in another sense I think that what some call the rash coward is a large and small weight; and in general every excess and deficiency is a large and small weight, for both are vices, and double measures. In yet another sense, the one who wants to be treated well by others but does not himself choose to give others rest in the same way has double measures, since he does not obey the commandment that says: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.”

It is not the ear that hears badly that is the Lord’s work, but the ear attentive to good things; and it is not the eye that sees badly that is the Lord’s work, but the eye that sees and pictures divine things. For whoever hears the Lord and looks to his commandments is the Lord’s work. The same must be said of the other parts of the body. You will use this saying against those who accuse this body of ours and insult God.

That is, do not sleep much, but be wakeful. Do not slander, so that you may not be carried off to Gehenna. Open the eyes of your soul through the virtues, and through wisdom be filled with spiritual breads.

For a person to hold himself in the balance between the works of the Lord and those of the devil is an abomination to the Lord. By “a deceitful balance” he means the mind, which by nature is meant to judge matters justly but swerves, through the inclination of its free will, for the sake of friends or money.

Do not be quickly moved, he says, to make a promise to God, lest, when need or the desire for more has often seized you, you begin to regret it and insult God by preferring something else to him. Regret over good things happens not to the just but to the unjust; so let the unjust promise nothing to God without thinking, for after vowing comes regret. — To make a hasty pledge to the Lord, that is, to consecrate something of one’s own, and then to regret it quickly, is a snare to a man.

Christ is the winnower of the ungodly; he will fall upon the ungodly like a lion upon prey. The wheel is that of the threshing floor, separating the chaff from the grain; or else the wheel he will bring upon them is inescapable punishment.

The storerooms of the belly are the mind, the heart and knowledge, where all teachings, both divine and impious, are laid up. And just as someone lights a lamp because he wants to find something lying in the storerooms, so the Lord, with the light of his knowledge, searches the storerooms of people in their words and deeds. For those who understand the knowledge of the Lord it is a light. If, then, the light of the Lord is the knowledge of the Lord, and the light of the Lord is the breath of human beings, then the knowledge of the Lord is the breath of human beings. But the devil, who seems to shine in ignorance, he called a lamp that empties the mind of good knowledge and disguises itself as an angel of light. And since the ungodly did not choose to know the light of the Lord or to walk in it, they counted ignorance as light; and if they held ignorance to be light, clearly they also did the works of the devil, the inventor of ignorance. Those who walked with him in his ignorance will be with him forever and ever; but those who walked in the knowledge of the Lord will be with the Lord.
CHAPTER 21
This saying rules out sacrifice by means of irrational animals; for the sacrifice to God is a broken spirit.

If the works of the Lord are pure and upright, and the mind too is one of his works, then the mind was created upright and pure by God, and we must keep it upright toward him against the evils that come upon us from the evil one.

He has set the whitewashed and common house over against the corner in the open air. If the whitewashed and common house is wickedness, the corner in the open air is virtue. A corner in the open air, then, is practice in touch with contemplation and illuminated by the Sun of righteousness. Paul too fittingly called the high priest of the Jews a whitewashed wall about to be struck (12) by God, and the Saviour in the Gospels called the Pharisees whitewashed tombs. He also did well to say “on a corner,” where lies the stone rejected by the builders, which became the head of the corner, who is Christ. And “common” is whatever does not belong to the one God.
A secret gift is what the right hand does while the left hand does not know. Whoever is sparing with gifts to the needy stirs up strong wrath against himself on the day of judgment.
The assembly of the giants is wickedness and ignorance, and the giants are the demons. That is, the one who wanders from the way of righteousness will rest in great sins.

It is better to be without a wife than to live with such a woman. And David says: “In a desert land, trackless and waterless, so have I appeared before you in the sanctuary.” A desert land, then, is the soul that has virtue and does not have the old men dwelling in it, who are corrupted according to the old desires of deceit. That is why the devil finds no rest in it either, since he wanders with difficulty through waterless places seeking rest and finds none; for he is king of all that is in the waters, that is, of those who are in the repose and enjoyment of fleshly pleasures. And again: “The dwellings of wisdom’s houses are dry.” If so, then the quarrelsome, talkative and angry woman is wickedness, which makes the one who lives with her quarrelsome, talkative and angry.
The wisdom of the Lord will rest in the heart of the righteous wise man; but foolish men slander it in order to corrupt it.

Wisdom is a fortified city in which the wise dwell, tearing down reasonings and every height raised up against the knowledge of God. — By fortified cities he means souls fortified and held in subjection by ungodly demons and wicked men, who raise themselves up against the knowledge of God. The wise man has scaled their stronghold and, fenced about by wisdom, has torn down their apparent security.
Whoever guards his mouth and tongue, his mind, his anger and his desire keeps his soul from affliction at the judgment.

He is one and the same man, conceived of in different ways. Bold is the one who does anything at all without fear; self-willed, the one who wants to act freely without discernment; boastful, the one who exalts himself beyond what he has; a pest, the one who not only harms himself but passes it on to others as well, for he is so harmful that he even imparts vices to others. And whoever bears a grudge is a transgressor.

For there is also good desire. It belongs to angels never to desire the desires of wickedness; to demons, always to desire evil things; to human beings, sometimes to desire and sometimes not. “All day long” stands for “through the whole of life.” The same is true of “Be in the fear of the Lord all day long,” which stands for “through the whole of life.”

By “horse” he means the mind, which is attacked by the devil and fights back. For it says: “You will mount your horses, and your riding is salvation.” And the Lord says concerning Paul: “to carry my name.”
CHAPTER 22

He called a good name the virtue signified by its proper name; for that name is truly good which has a good thing as what it signifies. Thus we will not praise an unjust woman who is called Justice, but the one who has justice, even if she is taken for Injustice. And above silver and gold is wisdom, [?] white.

They meet each other: the rich man by his almsgiving purging away his anger and acquiring love, and the other being taught humility through his poverty. For he wants the one to be instructed and the other to share, so that the one may be thankful and the other merciful.
Whoever has wisdom and the fear of the Lord will inherit heavenly life, glory and wealth. For Noah had all the generations; Abraham had these; and so did those who were made disciples by Peter.

In the age to come those who have been enriched in everything, in all knowledge and wisdom, will rule over the impure and over those deprived of this wealth. But who the servants are and who the masters, there is no need to make public, because the account of them is mystical and rather deep. Taken literally, the saying shows the instability of human life. But also in oligarchies the rich rule the poor. In another sense, those who have knowledge rule those who do not; and the believers from the Gentiles lend teaching to those from Israel, to whom they formerly gave orders [?]; although previously it was they who lent to many nations and ruled over them. But now that the kingdom has been taken from them, the reverse has come about.

God loves the man who is cheerful in keeping the commandments and a giver in almsgiving, as Paul too says: “He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” And the Lord brings to an end the vanity of his works through virtue and knowledge.
He calls the virtues of the soul a man’s gifts. By them he overcomes the devil, makes himself honoured before God, and takes his own soul away from the demons who had laid hold of it.

He wants the man to be driven out of the worst habit through spiritual teaching, together with the contentiousness he had. The devil, too, being a pest, must be driven out of the soul; for if he sits in it, he dishonours all right thoughts through his impurity. For the Apostle too shows that the soul is a council, by introducing thoughts that accuse or else defend: “their thoughts,” he says, “accusing or else defending one another”; and where there is accusation and defence, there is also a council. Moreover, the pest dishonours everyone, as an insolent man; or else, wanting to establish his own views, he casts out those of others with dishonour. Cast him out of the spiritual assembly. And not only will he himself be cast out, but also everything that goes with him: strifes, contentions, quarrels, and whatever makes a man a pest.

The Lord who keeps our souls is also the one who shepherds us with spiritual knowledge, coming down to us and saying, “I am the good shepherd,” the one whom the lawless man dishonours. And if Christ is king of those who are ruled and shepherd of sheep, he will one day be king alone of the sheep, when they have passed over to royal dignity.

Our enemy the devil prowls around like a lion, seeking someone to devour. Fearing him, the sluggard shrinks back from the work of the virtues.
