And if a lion, which is the devil, seeks to hunt someone in the ways of righteousness, then in the broad streets that lead to destruction he himself, with the phalanx of his demons, murders those who obey him.

The deep pit is the devil; and the one hated by the Lord is the one who does not keep careful watch over himself. Job was not hated by the Lord, but for the sake of testing he fell (13) into the mouth of the transgressor. But the one hated by the Lord is left in the pit to the end, being a lover of pleasure even though he knows his sin.
Far from the heart of the fool is the rod from the root of Jesse, Christ, who will shepherd his people, the new Israel, in the pasture of his own sheep.

Just as the devil slanders us before God, taking from us the virtues that he did not give us, so we too slander him, taking from him the vices that we did not give him. Insofar as we take the vices from him, we take as from one who is poor in virtues; but insofar as we give him our virtues to our own loss, we give as to one who is rich in wickedness. “Lest,” he says, “as one giving little to a ruler” [?]; with whom, by slandering, he gains more, but is harmed more in his soul.

Whoever attends to the all-wise words of God and does what he commands has applied his heart and knows that they are good. The one who hears the words of God is the one who does what they command; “for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” And if you apply your heart to knowing and doing, he will make known to you his way, which said: “I am the way and the truth.”

Whoever has enlarged his heart through purity will understand the words of God: the practical, the sapiential and the theological. For the whole subject matter of Scripture is divided in three: into ethics, natural philosophy and theology. Proverbs corresponds to the first, Ecclesiastes to the second, and the Song of Songs to the third. When these are understood through purity, they are written on the heart, so that you may answer—that is, so that you may be ready to make a defence to everyone who asks you for an account of the hope that is in you, whether in order to learn or in order to oppose. And you too should question in turn those who are able to be questioned; but do not put pressure on one who is poor in knowledge. That is why he adds: “And do not dishonour the weak man at the gates.”

Those who welcome base thoughts and thereby honour the evil one should strive with all their might to pay off the worse thoughts by means of good ones; for if they are not able to do this, they will have taken from them the bed under the sides of the soul, that is, virtue. — Whoever moves the boundaries of piety turns it into superstition or impiety; and whoever moves the boundaries of courage makes it into rashness or cowardice. The same must be understood of the other virtues, of the doctrines, and of the faith itself. But this must be observed above all with regard to the Holy Trinity: for whoever does not confess the Holy Spirit as God dissolves baptism, and whoever names some others as gods as well brings in a mob of gods. Or else: the ordinances of the fathers concerning each matter, which for that very reason ought to remain, must not be moved.
CHAPTER 23

Here he calls the devil a "ruler." His tables are false witness, abuse, slander, evil counsel, shameful desires, and every satanic practice of any kind. When the evil one sets these before you, understand them spiritually and apply your mind to them, for the mind is the "hand." Know that you must prepare the kind of things that ought to stand beside you on the day of the Lord, when he renders to each according to his works. But if you are rather insatiable, and long for lofty things, more and greater things, which are divine and of God. Do not desire the evil one's dishes, for these belong to a temporary life, that is, a false one. The divine Scripture must be understood intellectually and spiritually, for the knowledge that comes through the senses, according to the history, is not true (15).

If you try to drag the divine sense down to the letter, according to outward sight alone, it will not stand firm but departs to its own house, which is the contemplation proper to it. It has wings made for it by its master, the Holy Spirit, and these wings are the spiritual gifts. So it goes off on high, above the very ether, so to speak. Therefore, not to rise above the letter, but to be insatiable for these things, belongs to a false life.
The envious man eats the bread of impiety and gets drunk on the wine of lawlessness, and one must not dine with him. So one must not be impious and lawless, for these vices ruin spiritual knowledge.
"Say nothing intelligent," he says, that is, nothing deep and mystical, for you must not cast your pearls before swine.

Do not move the eternal boundaries of godliness. Do not enter the land of those who have made themselves orphans away from God, who hold vice, the property of demons, through which they were deprived of the heavenly Father. For the Lord who redeems them from darkness, the Lord of the surpassingly bright light, is strong.
An upright son will keep his lips busy with wisdom, and wisdom will converse with him and remain with him; but the crooked will fall away from her.
If it is by the fear of the Lord that one turns away from evil, he rightly urges us to turn away from every evil throughout our whole life.

Everyone who is drunk with vice, and everyone who goes whoring away from wisdom toward ignorance, will become poor in divine grace. And no one who drowses in the demonic night will put on the wedding garment; instead, his flesh, torn like a rag, will be crushed in the flame of Gehenna.

One of the elders said that the soul is the mother of the mind. By "soul" he meant the passible part of the soul, both the spirited part and desire. For through the practical virtues the soul brings the mind forth into the light: through courage and temperance, which are the virtues of the spirited part and of desire, we acquire wisdom and the knowledge of God. He might perhaps also call the Old Testament a mother not to be despised.

Here by "men" he means the writings of the teachers. Those who both did and taught, and made their journey toward heaven, he has named "walks." For many who taught did not make their journey toward heaven, because they did not keep what they taught. He who converses "in walks," that is, who both does and teaches, walks worthily of the calling to which he was called by God.

Sin in thought is like a bowl; sin in deed, like a cup. A "pestle" is what cooks call a pounder. This pestle knocks many times and does not open the place it knocks on. But the Lord says to his disciples, "Knock, and it will be opened to you."
A mind that has taken in a foreign thought or teaching will dwell on evil thoughts; but he who has kept himself will inherit life.

Insensibility is a terrible thing. Afterwards, stricken in conscience, you will say: "I did not take the trouble to see that I won the rewards and was delivered from the torments." "They mocked me," that is, they reproached me; "I did not know it," and that by my own will. [?] "Morning" is the dawn of the soul and the recognition of sin.
CHAPTER 24.
The house of the virtues is built with divine wisdom, and is set upright with understanding, the fear of God, and knowledge.

Whoever suffers shipwreck in faith or in any of the virtues has no helmsman for the war against the opposing powers, either in theology or in the virtues. But whoever wages war with a helmsman seems to have sense on earth. A counseling heart, which does everything with counsel, goes before the help of God. The same can be said of every virtue. There is shipwreck in temperance too, and in love, and in love of money, and in the same way shipwreck happens over each doctrine of the catholic and apostolic Church. If we must make war on our adversaries under a helmsman, then our life on earth is like a sea battle. If we are willing, we sink them by prayer of the heart and by a mind turned toward God; if we are unwilling, we are sunk. And even if they make war on us, however great and fierce their war may be, it is nothing. Let us only fence ourselves about with fasting and self-control, and we shall tear them and their weapons to pieces like a spider's web. And if, as the Lord said, "where two or three are"—the heart, the mind, and the soul—they agree to keep within his commandments, the Lord is with us.

Those who understand all that God does, and do all that he teaches, in no way transgress his word. The gates of the wise are the practical virtues and the contemplation of the mind, through which the wisdom of God enters. They turn aside neither to the right nor to the left, because they reason in councils about good and evil: the good they lay hold of, and the evil they hurl back.

Those who refuse to be instructed under the wisdom and knowledge of God meet eternal death by way of the present death. The fool is the one who has tasted the sweetness of the wisdom of God and then abandoned it and will join himself to folly; that is why he also died together with his sins. If vice diminishes virtue, then clearly virtue also destroys vice. This will happen in the age to come, until vice has died out. For "will be defiled" stands for "will be destroyed." Uncleanness is destroyed either by the practical life or by severe punishment.

This saying should be applied to those who have been counted worthy of divine knowledge, so that they do not neglect teaching while many are being led away by vice to death. Those who are being killed because of their innocence, do not hesitate to buy back with your own blood. Buy them back (16) by giving money or a profitable word. And if you say, "I do not know this man," he will convict you of lying, and you will be guilty of two things, namely lying and murder. For he who formed the breath himself knows all things, he who renders to each according to the quality of his deeds: good to the good, and evil to the wicked. That it is not according to quantity is clear: "For the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come." But if anyone wants to take it in terms of quantity, let him think of the recompense as proportionate to each person's capacity, just as the gifts of the Spirit too are given in proportion to faith.

Whoever profits from the divine Scriptures eats honey. But whoever draws out of them the principles of things, from which the holy prophets and the apostles took them in both doing and teaching, chews the honeycomb. Anyone who wishes may eat the honey, but only the pure may eat the honeycomb. Or else the allegory should be called honey, and the literal examination and the history the honeycomb, insofar as it holds the hidden and deeper sense, for the honey is inside the comb. The "throat" is the nourishing faculty of the soul, through which food is passed down to the belly. If then you succeed in these things, both what concerns the sense and what concerns the history, the wise doctrines themselves will give you perception of wisdom. For if you find the spiritual sense of Scripture, your end will be good, so that it may be said, "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints"; and you will not lose your hope for the future.

Do not prefer the devil to the righteousness of God, in which the righteous are pastured. Do not be deceived by deadly foolish talk into filling your heart, which is the "belly." — Do not betray God for the sake of pleasure, for he is the pasture of the righteous, and he will never forsake you.

God turns his anger away from the one who has fallen, having mercy on him; but he is angry with the one who exults over the fall of his enemy. For everyone who gloats over a soul that is perishing is like the devil, who does not want all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Indeed, the Lord in the Gospels has commanded us to pray for our enemies, that is, for men.

The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, is "not of flesh," meaning that it is not perceptible to the senses. Whoever has stumbled and is handed over to it will be crushed: his bones will be pounded by a pestle and obliterated, burned up by fire. Or else: whoever is handed over to it for repentance will be crushed like wheat by the word of its wisdom, so that he may become sweet bread. — Those who have been corrupted and have grown old according to the desires of deceit, the sword of God consumes to utter destruction. Or else: those who have come from vice to the knowledge of God it consumes "with their sinews," cutting them away from their wicked deeds, so that they may put off the old man and put on the new, created according to God. This new man is also not food for demons, since he has been cleansed by the Lord and abstains from all vice; for the text adds, "so that they are not food for the young of eagles." Or else it means that, once burned up and reduced to ashes, they are no longer food for the eagles. For "my words" are fenced about [?], and so on. — "Who has gathered the winds in his bosom?" Faith has gathered the mind, which is swifter than the wind, from east and west, from north and sea, into the knowledge of God, and has given them spiritual contemplation to store up in the virtues. For the knowledge of God is the bosom of God, in which he enfolds and holds fast all who think on God, as one holds gold in one's bosom. — The one who gathered all the earth-born nations from east and west, from north and sea, and knit them closely together with the virtues in faith in him, is Christ God. He also stored up the heavenly water that flows from the fountain of life, that is, knowledge and wisdom, as Christ himself says: "Whoever drinks of this water will never thirst"; and: "Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly." — The one who steals knowledge is not the one who takes from someone who went before him, but the one who filches from knowledge falsely so called. For all who have believed in Christ and receive contemplations from the holy prophets and apostles are not called thieves of other people's contemplations. One steals other people's contemplations in order to fill a hungry mind; but that happened before the coming of the Savior. Now Paul says: "Let the thief steal no longer, but rather let him work righteousness, so that, having acquired knowledge, he may share it with the one in need." For what is not ours, that we who have believed in Christ should steal it? All things are ours, and we are Christ's, through whom all things came to be, and Christ is God's. — Once the mind has fled from vice, do not hand it back over to vice, since everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. Here "sin" is the name given to the devil, who works sin. — "A wicked offspring," and so on. Blasphemy curses the mind that utters it, and does not bless its mother, that is, the soul. — Vainglory undermines and mocks the one who has it, leading him to count himself righteous, not reflecting on his evil deeds, but only on the good he often does. Pride makes the one who possesses it overlook poor friends, and likewise his parents; it makes him spurn wretched food [?], loathe the righteous and the pious, trip up those under his hand, and climb above them himself. Anger forces everyone who has it to do nothing but harm and punish, and he never stops slandering, insulting, and making false accusations.

Whoever looks with approval on a mind, his own or any other person's, that thinks wickedly and carries out its thoughts in action and contemplation will be accursed among the peoples of the angels and hated among those saved from the nations, when all will become one flock with one shepherd. But those who reprove and expose [?] their own deeds through confession, and the reflections of the better mind, will appear exalted before the Lord and will be proclaimed above all. In the present age the good blessing of practical deeds will come upon them, and the spiritual contemplation of wisdom; in the age to come, the portion allotted by the Lord. Whoever walks after the commandments of God is built up into righteousness and holiness. For with wisdom a house is built, in soul and body, as a dwelling place for God; but wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil.
Whether thorns or cattle, they ruin it if there is no one to clear it and guard it. So it is with the fool as well: vice is [?] the one that goads him toward the things that win the kingdom.
The wall is the dispassion of the rational soul, built up out of the practical virtues. It is torn down and destroyed by the fool's own choice.
CHAPTER 30 OF THE LATIN VULGATE.

Corruption loves these things: Hades, lust, and a harlot. These too have neither limit nor satiety. "There are three that will be filled [?], and the fourth was not content to say 'Enough'": Hades, and love of a woman, and earth not filled with water; and water and fire did not say, "It is enough." The earth always takes in seed: whatever you sow, it craves more. In the same way death and fire destroy whatever they crave. Poverty is something like this too; these things consume. Sloth and idleness are something like this as well. Someone might perhaps wonder why Hades is never satisfied, even though it devours man. That is why, he says, these things are never satisfied either, and never stop anywhere. And see how he has compared fornication to Hades.

These ravens mystically feed the righteous but punish the unrighteous, digging out the eyes of unrighteousness, because they mocked the Father and God of all and dishonored the ancient knowledge that gave them birth. The eye of the Father is the law given to us by him in righteousness. Those who dig out the eyes of the ungodly man he called ravens, and those who devour him entirely he named eagles, because the former have been entrusted with partial purification and the latter with complete purification. For God wills that even the ungodly be saved.

Among us the cock, the bird, is said to utter things unspeakable, but to the hens that live with it they are intelligible. The flocks of hens follow it, perhaps because they all go about it for the delight they take in it, and it is spirited in its love toward all of them. In the same way the ranks of angels yield to the God of all not only from fear but also from love (20), whenever he wishes them to understand his command and to do it. It is the same with the souls of the righteous. To those that are subject to his command he is pleased to make known not only the mysteries and depths stored up in the Scriptures, but also whatever is going to happen to people in this life, from men and from demons. He grants them foreknowledge of these things, either through a vision of the mind by the grace of the divine Spirit, or through initiation by an angel, or through revelation in a vision.
(CHAPTER 31 OF THE LATIN VULGATE)

Here he calls the righteous "rulers," because they have power over the demons and the passions, a power which he called "temper." Let them not drink the sour wine of the heretics, which intoxicates the mind and muddies the wits and holds something against the knowledge of God's wisdom. Otherwise, having drunk it, they may forget the wisdom of God and how to judge rightly and to understand the contemplation of knowledge, and may no longer be able to benefit their own souls or those of the weaker.

To those who are grieving in their sins and in despair, give drink from the Lord's vineyard until they are drunk, that is, fasting, prayer, self-control, confession, and everything that brings gladness to the soul. To those who are only beginning, give the pains of sin to drink their fill, so that, having drunk, they may forget the poverty that comes from the demons. For whoever has been made drunk with the knowledge of the Lord forgets the experience of his pains.
By "poor" he means one who is deprived of knowledge, and by "weak" one who is unclean with sins.
CHAPTER 25.

Whoever uses spiritual reason to starve the old self, which is being corrupted by deceitful desires, sets his own mind right in righteousness. The mind is said to be the throne of God, for wisdom, knowledge and righteousness can by their nature sit nowhere else but in a rational nature; and all these things are Christ.

Show yourself as you are and do not boast. Keep silent among the wise and listen among elders. Do not say, “I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High.” Do not long for the first place among the chief seats, but look to the lowest place. It is better for someone to say to you, “Come up to me,” than for you to be sent back to the lowest place in shame in front of a ruler. Do not proclaim yourself prudent or count yourself righteous. It is better for this to be said of you: “Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name.”

“Behind” means the things that happened before. God is our friend: out of his friendship toward us he became man. He himself said to the disciples, “I no longer call you servants, but friends.” Whenever your friend, Christ, reproaches you because of sin and tells you to keep away from it, do not despise him. Turn back and return to your first temperance, that is, to God’s love for humankind.

By “grace” he means God’s commandments, and by “friendship” love toward God and neighbour. Whoever loves God should keep them within himself, so that he will not stand reproached before God when God gives each person what he deserves. In the Gospels the Saviour says to the Jews who had believed in him, “If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples”; and the truth has set us free from the curse of the law. If friendship sets us free, then the Saviour sets us free; and Christ is the truth and the friendship. So all who have knowledge of Christ are friends of one another. In this friendship alone, those who are friends of the same one are also friends of others.
Whoever has been taught about the virtues and practises them guards his own affairs with fair dealing.
Set a costly sardius in a golden earring, and the wisdom of the Lord in a mind that is free of passion and obedient to the Lord.

Water flowing from snow at harvest time in the heat is helpful and cools the scorching heat. God is like this to those who receive knowledge and wisdom and his commandments. And as heat melts snow, so a righteous person’s advice melts the wickedness of the soul.

Winds and clouds are the plainest warnings to sailors, so that they will not be shipwrecked. False knowledge is the same for those who live in the wisdom of God, so that they will not perish with those who boast in it.

Bones give the body strength and secure its vigour, and virtues naturally do the same for the soul. A soul that does not keep watch breaks these bones by its sins. Some have called the irascible soul “soft”: it breaks its own spiritual bones that face toward God, the bones that by nature say, “Lord, Lord, who is like you?”
The way of the evil man is wickedness, and the foot of the lawless man is lawlessness; and it will perish on the day of judgment. “Way” should be understood as a habit, and “foot” as an activity.

Vinegar is food and gives pleasure, yet it does harm in the wound of someone whose wound has begun to fester. In the same way, looking at a woman and talking with her tears at the heart of a man who has given himself to virtue and is only beginning. For the passion that strikes the heart is wickedness, and some are called passionless because they are free of it. — Perishable grief is the loss of perishable pleasure, but praiseworthy grief is the loss of the virtues and of the knowledge of God.

Here “bread” means the solid food of the soul, the commandments, and “drink” signifies divine knowledge. “Coals of fire” are the gifts of the all-holy Spirit, which set people ablaze and burn away their wrinkles. Once a seraph touched Isaiah’s lips with a coal of fire, and once cleansed, Isaiah cried out to all, “Learn righteousness.” When you cleanse your neighbour’s ruling faculty through this kindness and beneficence, the fire-bearing graces of the Holy Spirit will press upon him. He will not only accept them; you will also make him imitate you in every good work, since he has become your sponsor among all the friends of God.

He has called the devil an “impudent face.” The devil provokes the soul to wickedness and stirs up evil thoughts in it, as the north wind stirs up clouds. Everywhere Solomon uses “tongue” for the mind. So it is not good to show respect to this face in judgment.

Here a righteous mind falls before Satan when it accepts an unclean thought or a false doctrine. A person stops up the fountain of wisdom by turning away from its knowledge, and he fouls the outlet of the knowledge of God. Some of the mind’s thoughts are called falls, others risings, others sitting, others standing, and others walking. Some of them are called stumbling blocks, others hard and soft, fragrant and foul-smelling, sweet and bitter, smooth and straight, and crooked. Again, some are called thorns and thistles, others light and darkness, life and death, others sickness and health, and others again falsehood and truth. Scripture gives many other names both to the soul and to its thoughts. A few of the many can be mentioned: mind, soul, heart, human being, man, woman, slave, household servant, father, son, spirit, eye, mouth, lips, tongue, throat, belly, bosom, arm, finger, nostril, sheep, kid, shepherd, and many more names of the soul, which cannot be set out one by one now.

Here he has used “counsel” for the inclination of the heart toward what is better. Someone may fail to call on God’s help within himself, though that help is the counsel by which he would do some good thing with careful thought. If he begins instead in self-will and boasting, his work will not be finished; whatever he attempts will collapse, because he has not walled himself around with God’s help as his counsel.
Chapter 26.

Here “horse” means a person who is quick to learn wisdom and open to righteousness; he whips such a person with riddles. “A goad for the donkey” means goading someone who is slow in these matters with harsh words and making him afraid. By saying that “a foolish nation” is beaten “with a rod,” he means servants or subjects who have no sense, for the rod is a symbol of punishment.

“From his feet,” and so on. Here “feet” means the servants. A master brings reproach on himself through them when he sends word by a foolish messenger, whether the message is counsel, wisdom, an embassy, an alliance, or words of sympathy. The fool fails in everything. Indeed the Lord says in the Gospels, “One must not give what is holy to dogs, or throw pearls before swine.”
Remove the evil way from the fool, and put false knowledge far away from him.
Whoever shares knowledge with a fool is like someone who fixes a worthless stone in a golden sling, or who pelts someone with a precious stone from a slinging sling.

If the estrangement of fools, by which they turned away from God, is broken, they become pure again and draw near to God, “for all flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Note here that he has called souls made coarse by wickedness “the flesh of fools.” So too the Lord says, “My spirit shall not remain among human beings, because they are flesh.”
Whoever has thrown off his wickedness, he says, and then returns to it, is like a dog that eats its own vomit. Lot’s wife was like this, and so was the man to whom the unclean spirit returned.

This saying should be used against those who vote unworthy people into the priesthood or the clergy. None of us established the just judgment and the freedom of the Church, and it does not belong to us. It belongs to Christ, who judged it right to give himself to be slaughtered for its sake and to have his blood poured out for it. So everyone who wants to be entrusted with the helm of the Church must give himself up, seize the tail of the evil one, set free those held under his wickedness, and bring them to the knowledge of Christ.

As fire flourishes and burns in wood, so the mind’s anger, turned toward the passions, flourishes and burns in evil thoughts. But where there is no one who is double-minded (that is, double-souled), [?] either God or mammon, then what belongs to the other will be quieted in him. Either God’s command prevails and the evil one’s melts away, or [?] he will make peace with wickedness. But if he chooses both, he will fall away from life and also lose the things of this passing time.

Here “lips” means thoughts. Some people do not open the lips of the mind against the evil one by confessing to God the evil things he may have sown in them against God. Whoever hides these things instead covers his own heart with grief. In his folly he does not think he has any sin in them, and he does not know God’s compassion: God gives crowns all the more to those who endure in this way and declare these things to him, as to those who struggle for his sake every day.
Chapter 27.

He has used “mocks” in place of “rejoices.” A pure soul delights in the knowledge of the Scriptures and rejoices as it is filled. But an impure soul thinks that even knowledge falsely so called is entirely true.

The place of the heart is virtue and knowledge. A person who becomes estranged from them falls into wickedness and ignorance, and by committing sin becomes its slave. For since he is rational, his place is virtue.

A mind free of passion delights in many kinds of things: wisdom, knowledge and the singing of hymns. A mind ruled by passion is torn apart in ignorance and wickedness, and it comes to a great fall that is hard to heal.

God is our friend, and the friend of the fathers of old and of those after us. He himself said, “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves broken cisterns.” — Here the brother is Christ, by grace. The commandments he has given us are our right to enter his house, that is, the kingdom of heaven. Do not enter your brother’s house without them, unless you have obtained them. The man who came into the wedding feast without a wedding garment was like this: he was bound hand and foot and thrown out of the wedding. — Here our brother is the choir of angels. Before his transgression and fall, the devil, by the nature of angels, was a brother of the angels and of us; but God is our friend. It is better to live near and close to the one who is nearer, our true God and friend, than to yield, as if to a brother, to the devil, who has put himself far from God, and so to perish with him. — The one joined to me through true knowledge is better than the one joined to me only through nature.
A person’s house is virtue. If he does not take diligent care of it, he falls away from it in times of temptation.

Here the fig tree is the righteousness of God. Those who plant it in themselves and give cuttings of it to others will eat its fruit from the hand of the Lord, who alone is righteous and who awards the prize of righteousness. He ranks those who have kept his righteousness with himself and grants them the righteousness that also justifies the angels, in the unchanging splendour of righteousness. Whoever keeps the word of the Lord keeps the Lord in his heart, so that the Lord cannot be separated from him. He will be honoured not only here by the angels, but also in the age to come by the Creator of the angels.

That is: you will not turn a fool away from folly by dishonouring him, but by teaching him what kind of dishonour folly brings on him. A rebuke to someone’s face makes the sinner more shameless. — Some of God’s words have been written for the life of sons, and others for the life of servants.
Chapter 28.

If there is a man who is bold in impiety, there is also one bold in virtue. If the man bold in impiety slanders the poor, the man bold in virtue encourages the poor. So everyone who urges the poor to join him in impiety slanders them before God, that is, accuses them in turn, so that they will perish with him.

A violent rain not only destroys the crops but also washes away the face of the earth that yields them. There is also a gentle rain, which makes the face of the earth flourish and feeds the crops in it and gives them life. The violent rain kills people by destroying the crops, while the gentle rain gives life through the crops.

There is a lawless law and a just law. The lawless one destroys those who obey it. The just one not only gives length of days but also wins the kingdom of heaven for those who submit to it, because it is God’s. Everyone who loves God loves his law and does what the law requires, and everyone who keeps the law gains freedom from passion and the knowledge of God. And if those who love the law set a wall around themselves, then here “wall” means freedom from passion and the knowledge of God, which alone by nature can guard the rational nature.
If the wealth of the impious is wickedness, and wise men will destroy it, then clearly the righteous and wise destroy wickedness by leading the impure back to virtue through spiritual teaching.

It is not the law that abhors someone’s prayer. It is God, who gave the law, who abhors the prayer of the one who turns his ear away and will not listen to the law. Paul likewise says, “Scripture, foreseeing what was to come,” meaning “He who gave Scripture foresaw what was to come.”

The evil one sows evils in a person’s heart. Whoever does not declare them to the Lord God or to a God-loving person will not prosper in winning victory over the evil one. But whoever declares them will be loved by God and by his angels. James says, “Confess your trespasses to one another, so that you may be healed,” and the Psalmist said, “I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my heart.”

The revenues of the evil king are vices and false doctrines, for those he rules pay these to him as revenue. Those who obey the evil one are accused before God, because they are subject not to God but to his enemy, the devil. Since God hates the devil for his evil works, the devil in turn slanders human beings before God by means of his own works. But whoever hates to wrong his own soul will live through the long time of the endless age.

Here he calls the devil a murderous man. Whoever stands surety for injustice stands surety for Satan, who promises him that he will pay back the fruits of injustice. — The lawless nation is the doctrines of demons, which the well-instructed son does not obey; and by “son” he means the mind. Whoever holds back his mind so that it is not thrown into the wickedness of the evil nation wins for his own soul an imperishable ornament for its neck, from the hand of the Lord.

Whoever cleanses himself of the passions and carries out God’s commandments will be filled with the bread of wisdom and knowledge of God, which nourishes the soul. But whoever seeks idleness so as not to do God’s commandments will be filled with poverty.

Those who are merciful now will receive mercy from God in the age to come and become angels, and they will rule over the envious and the impious rich. The Lord promised to give his disciples such an honour: they would sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. A throne is that in which the mind sits, full of spiritual knowledge, gathering together those who have strayed from godliness. Here “to judge” means “to teach,” as also in “Open your mouth with the word of God, and judge all things soundly,” where “judge” stands for “teach.” We should also know that when the merciful man prevails over the envious man, he will not become envious himself; rather, he will make the envious man merciful.

If the impious put away their impiety, they will become righteous. Here “destruction” means the removal of impiety. So too the Lord made Matthew “perish” from the tax booth and granted him righteousness. The righteous increase in number when the impious abandon their impiety and become righteous along with the righteous. But the righteous groan and are pained when they see the impious standing in the place of impiety and not repenting.
Chapter 29.

[?] of the Lord who rebukes, or the man who with a hard heart gives advice and promises to share the pleasures of wickedness with someone. Such a man is suddenly set ablaze by his craving for the passions, and then the death that comes upon all overtakes those who are his partners in them, and there is no healing for their soul. He did not say that there will be no healing once the flame has died down. He said that there will be no healing while the man is burning, since he clearly still has the fuel of the passions: wood, hay, straw. For health naturally comes to those who are burned once the cautery is over.

When the Lord praises the righteous on the day of judgment, the peoples who share their portion will rejoice. But all who are under the principalities and powers and the world-rulers of this world will surely groan then.

Here he calls God “father.” The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ rejoices when he sees those who are called by Christ’s name and who follow and imitate him in deed, word and wisdom. A shepherd is a good mind that possesses passionless thoughts. If so, a kid is a passionate thought and a sheep is a passionless thought. That is why the Lord sets the kids on his left and the sheep on his right; by “kids” he means those who possess passionate thoughts. In the same way he called those who have the weeds “weeds,” and those who have the wheat “wheat,” naming them after their worst or best habit. Paul’s saying “Love does not boast” is of the same kind; it stands for “the one who has love.”
Christ raises up the rational nature through his commandments, but the lawless Antichrist stirs up the human race toward destruction.

In every case, “to judge” is used for “to teach.” Someone who judges between two or more people about a single matter teaches what is just and teaches them to keep away from injustice. In the same way, with regard to the virtues and to anything good at all, “to judge” has been used for “to teach.” Here the man who judges nations is Peter, who taught the whole world faith in Christ and piety, and also Paul and the teachers who came after them. The worthless man means people like Theudas and Judas, and the man of Samosata, and those who think as they do. David says of the worthless man, “And they will laugh at him and say, ‘Look at the man who did not make God his helper.’”

The men of blood are the demons, who killed those living in Christ by shedding their blood. “But the upright will seek out his soul”: these are the people who want to do and understand what those martyrs did and understood.

Truly the fool cannot restrain his anger. The wise man, though, stores it up in part, that is, he is angry only about things that deserve it. That is the explanation to give to simpler people. To the more advanced, the wise man is the one who uses up his anger little by little through long-suffering.
For those who have kept the law, the Lord will be an interpreter in the kingdom. For those who have broken the law there will be no interpreter, but there will be a punisher.

The words “For even if he understands, he will not obey” show that no one is hard by nature. Someone hard by nature would never understand anything rightly. I say this because of Pharaoh, who was hardened against Israel and was disciplined not by words but by plagues.

Living in luxury makes a person sin, and everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. So everyone who lives in luxury is a slave of sin, and on the last day he will grieve over himself more than a little.

The Lord humbles the insolent, but he gives glory to the humble. — By “insolence” he means wickedness. On the day of judgment, wickedness brings insolence and the humiliation of destruction on those who practise it. But the humble-minded will be glorified by the glory they gave to God in hymns and in keeping his commandments, for to do his commandments is to glorify God. As the Lord himself says, “But those who glorify me I will glorify.” Wickedness brings outrage on a rational soul.

By “thief” he means no one other than the devil. Whoever divides himself, keeping part of God’s commandments but doing part of what the evil one commands, hates his own soul. The devil steals him little by little until he has stolen him completely, and then sacrifices him to himself. For “the thief,” he says, “comes only to steal and to kill and to destroy.” — By “oath” he means the law. As an oath places God in the soul, so the law brings God into the soul. And as perjury removes God from the soul, so lawlessness drives God out of it. So, he says, if they hear the law that has been given and do not confess their sins, because they fear people and are ashamed before them, they will be tripped up and fall into destruction. David says the same: “I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my heart.” And again: “Tell your sins first, so that you may be justified.” And Solomon says, “Whoever covers up his impiety will not be loved.”

All of us who carry out the commandments serve the angels. They are our leaders, who took charge of us from the beginning, when the Most High divided the nations and set their boundaries according to the number of his angels. If we serve the angels who lead us, in accordance with the Lord’s will, we will receive justice from the Lord in the judgment on that day when he judges the world in righteousness, since the Father has given all judgment to the Son.
Chapter 31.
Courage is the best state of the rational soul, the state by which it has overcome the enemies that oppose it.

Once we have conquered the opposing power, we strip it of its spoils by learning the principles that concern it. In this way, by exposing its evils, we ensure that people stay clear of its snares: not only will the simpler ones escape it, but those who have been carried off as its captives will easily get free.

The soul spins wool and linen when it trains itself in the principles of animate and inanimate things. Or it does so when it examines the principles of the practical life and of natural contemplation. Or it does so when it draws to itself the contemplation of bodies and of incorporeal beings, through the state it has gained by the practical life.

And the soul that rises while it is still night is found watchful by the Bridegroom, the Sun of righteousness. It is surely also praying not to fall into temptation, and saying, "I kept watch, and became like a sparrow alone on a housetop." The food of the soul is the study of the divine words, and its tasks are the virtues.
